issues.issue: "You, as successor-in-interest to DeNovo Music Group, Inc. and Steemer Corporation, respectively" uses "respectively" for a single addressee and two predecessor entities, leaving unclear which rights and obligations passed to the individual. It also leaves unstated whether "you" is the "Grantor", the "Artist", or both under the underlying Agreement.

The preamble merges the addressee into a single "you", yet operative paragraph 6.01(b)(i) (c012) conditions the first advance instalment on receipt of the agreement "fully executed by Grantor and Artist", treating them as two persons. The identification of the contracting party is therefore not squared with the operative payment trigger.

The clause says the Live Album "shall be comprised entirely of Master Recordings embodying Artist's 'live' concert performances" recorded in the Soviet Union, yet the same sentence continues "as well as two ... recordings embodying ... performance[s]", which cannot be reconciled with "entirely". The interlineated/garbled added words make the permitted content of the Live Album genuinely uncertain.

The list of albums subject to the 120-day deadline omits the first Album of the first Option Period, so it is arguable whether that omission is deliberate (because clause (ii) fixes a May 29, 1989 date) or an oversight. The garbled enumeration compounds which albums the 120-day rule reaches.

The fixed May 29, 1989 delivery date sits against paragraph 3.06(b) (c004), which requires the Live Album to consist of February 1989 Soviet concert recordings plus additional recordings; whether the date survives if the additional recordings are not then available is left unaddressed. Read with the 120-day rule in 4.01(a)(i) (c006) the two deadlines govern different albums, but the boundary depends on c004's content requirement.

The advance table is keyed to "First Album" through "Ninth Album" in sequence, but the operative text identifies albums by Contract Period, so matching a particular album to "the applicable amount set forth below" requires an inference the clause does not supply. If any period's albums are not delivered the sequence numbering becomes contestable.

The first instalment is triggered by PRI's receipt of "this agreement, fully executed by Grantor and Artist", but the amendment is a 1989 letter while the advance relates to the Initial Period album under the 1985 Agreement, so "this agreement" is ambiguous as between the two documents. The "First Sixty Days" proviso then runs from that ambiguous date.

"All Recording Costs or other costs in connection with making Master Recordings" pairs a defined term with an open-ended "other costs" catch-all whose reach (e.g. mixing, mastering, travel, video production) is undefined. The general words are not confined by any enumerated list.

Making Grantor responsible for all Recording Costs sits awkwardly with paragraph 6.01(b)(i) (c011-c014), under which PRI pays advances in instalments tied to commencement of recording and mixing, and with paragraph 8(c) (c027), under which PRI's own video costs become Advances. Whether the advances are the exclusive funding source is not resolved.

"Any and all monies payable hereunder, except mechanical royalty payments" leaves "hereunder" ambiguous as between this amendment letter and the underlying Agreement, and the single carve-out invites an expressio unius argument about other protected payments. The scope of the deduction right therefore turns on words the clause does not define.

The royalty is 19% of "the lowest wholesale price ... payable by PRI's customers", a base that is undefined for licensing or non-wholesale exploitations of Audio-Visual Devices. "Net Sales" and "lowest wholesale price" together leave the computation open where there is no conventional wholesale customer.

Sub-paragraph (a) covers only devices "sold by PRI", while 7.11(b) and 7.11(c) (c018, c019) cover sales by "PRI and/or its affiliates", so United States sales by an affiliate arguably fall outside every rate. The asymmetry is only visible when the three sub-paragraphs are read together.

The territories are enumerated exhaustively ("United Kingdom, West Germany, France, Canada, Benelux, Australia, New Zealand and Japan") with no catch-all, and terms such as "Benelux" and "West Germany" have shifting geographic content over the life of the deal. Which country a sale is "for distribution in" is left to be determined.

The percentage rate in this sub-paragraph is struck through and interlineated so that the operative number cannot be read from the face of the document ("...eight percent (   )"). A rate that cannot be determined is a mechanical defect going to the core of the obligation.

This residual rate applies "outside of the United States and the territories referred to in paragraph 7.11(b)", so its operation depends entirely on the closed territory list in 7.11(b) (c018) and, where the seller is not an affiliate, leaves the same coverage gap as 7.11(a) (c017). The three sub-paragraphs do not exhaustively allocate every sale.

The rate applies to "Records ... in the form of CD/Videos", a category defined in paragraph 13.04(g) (c029) and expressly excluded from "Audio-Visual Devices" by paragraph 13.03(a) (c028); a product falling between those definitions has no rate. The boundary between the 19%/12% audio-visual rates and this 12% CD/Video rate depends on those two definitions.

The fraction is built from "the royalty rate set forth in this agreement for Net Sales of disc Albums" in the applicable country, but this amendment letter sets out no disc Album rates, so "this agreement" must mean the underlying Agreement. Where a country has escalating or configuration-specific rates, which single "rate" feeds the numerator is unresolved.

The cross-reference is to "paragraph 13.15(a)(H) below", a sub-paragraph designation that does not exist as written and is in any event in the Agreement rather than "below" in this letter. The garbled citation leaves the "automatic free goods" being excluded unidentified.

PRI may exploit or refrain from exploiting the Concert Video "as it deems appropriate in its sole discretion", with no good-faith or best-efforts benchmark, and "editing ... for promotional and/or commercial purposes" is open-ended. The extent of the artist's residual protection turns on unstated limits.

An unfettered right to shelve the Concert Video is difficult to reconcile with paragraph 8(c) (c027), which charges all Concert Video costs to the artist as Advances recoupable against audio-only Record royalties, and with paragraph 8(a) (c025) deeming the purchase to discharge PRI's 5.02(a)(ii) production obligation. Read together the artist may bear the cost of a product PRI need never exploit.

The proviso states that "only fifty percent (50%) of such costs shall be recoupable from audio-only Record royalties" but says nothing about the other fifty percent, leaving it open whether that half is recoupable solely from audio-visual income or not recoupable at all. "All amounts paid by PRI in connection with the Concert Video" is also an open-ended cost category.

Costs incurred under a separate agreement with Red Star Entertainment are deemed "Advances under the Agreement", which must be squared with paragraph 6.01(b) (c011) fixing the Advances per Album and with paragraph 6.01(b)(ii) (c015) allocating recording costs to Grantor. How this extra Advance interacts with the fixed advance schedule is not stated.

"All forms of reproductions of Audio-Visual Recordings ... now or hereafter known, manufactured or distributed primarily for home and/or juke box use and/or use on or in means of transportation" pairs an open futurity phrase with a specific list of end-uses, so whether later technologies (digital video downloads, streams) qualify is genuinely contestable. "Primarily for home ... use" is itself a vague qualifier applied to media that did not exist in 1989.

The definition excludes "CD/Video", which is separately defined in paragraph 13.04(g) (c029) as a laser-read compact disc; a reproduction that is neither a disc nor plainly a home-use device falls into neither definition and so attracts no rate under 7.11 or 7.12. The two definitions must be read together to see the gap.

"A Phonograph Record in laser-read compact disc form embodying Audio-Visual Recordings, which may ... include additional audio-only Sides" is tied to a single 1989 physical format, leaving whether functionally equivalent later formats are CD/Videos unresolved. The permissive "may ... include additional audio-only Sides" also does not say how a mixed disc is royalty-treated.

The definition of "or equivalent" is circular and open-ended: "every form of pre-recorded tape, compact disc or any other Record equivalent" defines the term by using the word being defined, and the catch-all sits against two enumerated physical configurations, squarely raising ejusdem generis. Whether a non-physical format is an "other Record equivalent" cannot be resolved from the words.

"Except as expressly or by necessary implication modified hereby" makes the survival of every unamended term depend on the undefined and highly contestable notion of modification "by necessary implication". The closing words "without limitation or exception" pull against that very qualification.

This ratification must be reconciled with the letter's opening words, "Notwithstanding anything to the contrary expressed or implied herein", and with the several "notwithstanding" overrides in paragraphs 2, 3, 5 and 8(b); which text prevails where the amendment and the Agreement diverge is left to implication. The instrument thus supplies two competing priority rules.
